name: service-proxy
intent: Front a messaging service with a proxy that preserves the service's interface exactly while intercepting every exchange, so routing, security and observability policy can be changed independently of the service and of its callers.
problem: Cross-cutting delivery concerns - TLS and authentication, retries and failover, throttling, tracing, reply handling, version mediation - must be added to a service that many heterogeneous callers already depend on. Modifying the service couples it to infrastructure concerns and cannot help unmodifiable or legacy callers; giving each caller its own copy of the logic duplicates configuration, drifts apart over time and leaves most of the fleet unprotected.
context: Message-based or service-oriented integration where a service is reached through a remote interface or a message channel, where callers are numerous, heterogeneous (different languages, frameworks, teams) or cannot be recompiled, and where the runtime allows one additional component in the request path - an in-process wrapper, a co-located sidecar or a shared gateway - whose behaviour can be steered out of band.
benefits: Interface equivalence: callers keep the interface, protocol and code they already use, so cross-cutting behaviour is added without touching a single requestor.
One interception point per service: policy is written once and every caller gets it - including legacy, third-party and future ones - regardless of language or framework.
Controllability: routes, timeouts, retries, rate limits, certificates and mirroring rules change by configuration from a control plane instead of by redeploying the service.
The service keeps a single responsibility: delivery, security and observability concerns live at the boundary instead of spreading through business code.
Observability becomes uniform and complete: every exchange can be measured, traced, logged or selectively stored at the proxy without instrumenting each caller.
Safe evolution of an unchanged service: canary and shadow traffic, version mediation and kill switches are applied in front of it.
Ownership can be delegated: a specialized team can own the proxy and its policies without owning the service's business logic.
tradeoffs: An extra hop on every request path: additional latency and serialization cost, and one more component that must be at least as available as the service - it is now a single point of failure on the critical path.

A new runtime and control plane to operate: deployment, certificates and configuration distribution must be versioned, reviewed and rolled back, and a bad route or retry policy has fleet-wide blast radius.

Interface equivalence is a permanent maintenance obligation: the proxy is a second implementation of the contract, so every interface, IDL or schema change must be regenerated or re-implemented, and a proxy that 'mostly' matches fails at runtime instead of at compile time.
Transparent retries and failover are unsafe unless every operation is idempotent; a proxy that retries blindly duplicates side effects and amplifies load on a downstream that is already failing.

Behaviour hides in the path: debugging spans an extra component, timeouts and retries may be applied twice (caller and proxy), payload inspection costs CPU, and buffering in the proxy can break streaming.
Identity and context must be propagated explicitly (credentials, deadlines, tracing context, opt-out headers) or the backend loses the principal and budget it used to see.

It is a privileged target: a component that terminates TLS and sees every message must be hardened and kept current, and once TLS ends at the proxy the internal hop is plaintext unless it is separately protected.

participants.responsibility: The contract that both the service and the proxy honour - an abstract interface, an IDL-generated stub, a protocol or a documented message contract. It is the equivalence anchor: the requestor never learns that a proxy exists.

Implements the service interface, passes every exchange through to the real service, and applies the local policy (observability, security, retries, throttling, reply handling) without changing the observable contract.
The real subject: the messaging service or endpoint that performs the work. It stays unaware of the proxy and of the policies that are applied in front of it.
Client, neighbouring service or channel consumer that invokes the interface; it addresses the proxy instead of the service, and its code, credentials and error handling stay unchanged.

The ordered set of per-exchange handlers (authentication, tracing, rate limiting, retry, routing, redaction) that the proxy runs around the delegated call; new control means a new link, not an edit to the service.

Out-of-band channel that distributes the proxy's steering data - routes, timeouts, limits, certificates, mirroring rules, feature switches. This is what makes the fronted interface controllable at runtime rather than compiled in.

use_cases: Adding TLS/mTLS, authentication and audit logging in front of a legacy or third-party service that cannot be modified or recompiled.
Giving every caller of a service uniform retries, circuit breaking, deadline propagation and metrics by keeping the policy in one co-located proxy instead of in N client libraries.

Request-reply tracking in a messaging flow: the proxy stores the Return Address supplied by each requestor, substitutes its own reply channel and routes replies back to the original requestor (the Enterprise Integration Patterns Smart Proxy form).
Canary or shadow deployment of a new service version: the proxy routes or mirrors a share of the traffic while callers and the service remain unchanged.
Version mediation: expose the interface a caller was compiled against while translating to the service's current version (or the reverse) inside the proxy.
Tenant-level throttle or quota enforcement that operations can retune during an incident without a service release.
In-process client proxy: wrapping a service client behind the service interface so that all call sites share one timeout, retry and tracing policy.

Uniform mTLS, retries, timeouts, telemetry and canary routing for every polyglot workload without touching application code: Istio injects an Envoy proxy as a sidecar beside each service and steers it out-of-band via xDS configuration - the production-scale form of the interface-preserving front, with the mesh control plane as the Control Plane participant.

Delegating per-request authorization to an external service at the proxy instead of the backend: Envoy's ext_authz filter asks an external gRPC/HTTP authorizer before every request and returns 403 without ever reaching the service, so the security team owns the policy and the service stays unchanged.

In-process RPC form: gRPC client and server interceptors wrap every call on the channel with shared logging, retry, timeout, validation and auth policy (e.g. the grpc-ecosystem go-grpc-middleware chain), so all call sites honour one policy while callers and callees keep coding against the generated service interface.
avoid_when: A single language and a single team consume the service: a client library that each caller applies is simpler, adds no hop and is the standard alternative whenever latency matters.
The platform already fronts the service with a service mesh, API gateway or ingress that terminates TLS, retries and routes; a second proxy layer duplicates policy and doubles the failure surface.
The per-request budget is tight enough that an extra hop is measurable, or the traffic is extremely chatty - the proxy's cost is per exchange.

The policy must reason about business objects or transactional state in-process; a proxy only sees the wire contract, so that logic belongs in the service or in a client library that can see the domain.
The operation is non-idempotent and at-most-once semantics are required: do not hide retries or failover in a proxy; control it in the caller, or make the receiver idempotent first.
anti_patterns: A proxy that only 'mostly' mirrors the service interface - hand-written forwarders that miss a member or lag behind a contract change, so callers discover the gap as a production failure instead of a compile error.
Policy creep: business rules, payload shaping or domain validation migrating into the proxy until it becomes a hidden second service that no team owns and no test covers.
Blind transparent retrying or mirroring in the proxy, producing duplicate side effects and retry amplification against a downstream that is already failing.
Rolling out control-plane configuration without review, canary or rollback, so one bad route or limit affects every caller at once.
Terminating TLS and credentials at the proxy and then treating the internal hop, the proxy's logs and its identity as trusted - turning it into a plaintext vantage point and an attribution gap.
Using the proxy to hide a versioning problem forever: every translation widens the divergence instead of converging on one canonical contract.
design_principles: Program to an interface, not an implementation: the equivalence guarantee is only as strong as the shared contract both sides honour.
Single responsibility and separation of concerns: the service owns business behaviour, the proxy owns delivery, security and observability policy.
Open/closed: new policies arrive as interceptors or configuration while the service and its callers stay closed for modification.
Substitution transparency: the proxy must be substitutable for the service, including its error taxonomy, idempotency and ordering semantics.
A single point of control is also a single point of failure: take the coupling deliberately and operate the proxy as production-critical infrastructure.
Make the implicit explicit: everything the proxy does out of band (retries, rewrites, redaction, identity substitution) must be observable and documented.
best_practices: Derive the proxy from the same contract artifact as the service (IDL, schema, interface) and regenerate rather than hand-maintain forwarders, so equivalence stays mechanical.
Preserve observable semantics deliberately - same error taxonomy, same deadline behaviour, same ordering, at-most-once effects - and document every intentional difference.
Keep policy declarative, versioned and reviewable in one place; roll it out per service with a canary and a tested rollback path, never as a hot edit.
Bound everything the proxy adds: propagated deadlines, capped retries with idempotency keys, circuit breakers and bulkheads, so the proxy cannot amplify an outage.
Propagate identity, deadline and tracing context, and give callers an override/opt-out channel (headers, metadata) to escape retries or mirroring.
Treat the proxy as a trust boundary: mTLS on both sides, authorization decisions bound to the propagated principal, and payloads redacted before they reach logs or a message store.
Monitor the proxy itself - added latency, queue depth, error rate, active configuration version - because it now sits on the critical path of every request.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Smart Proxy (System Management chapter), with Request-Reply and Return Address for the messaging form.
Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Proxy, the in-process ancestor of the same interface-preserving delegation.
